---
title: "Post-Processing Results"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(PKNCA)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
conflicted::conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter, dplyr::select, .quiet = TRUE)
```

## Why post-process?

After `pk.nca()` you may need to:

1. **Extract** results as a tidy data frame for further analysis
2. **Exclude** specific results that failed QC (poor half-life fit, protocol deviation)
3. **Normalize** parameters by dose (built-in `.dn` variants)
4. **Summarize** with custom statistics, respecting exclusions
5. **Report** with the `business.*` summary helper functions
6. **Inspect** which concentrations each λz regression used, and the fitted line

Data-quality checks that run before or alongside exclusion (missing samples, Tmax coverage, input validation) are covered in the [Data Quality Checks chapter](data-quality.qmd).

Most of this operates on the `PKNCAresults` object without rerunning the analysis (requesting `.dn` parameters is the exception — they are computed by `pk.nca()`). The package's own [Post-Processing vignette](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v07-post-processing.html) walks the same workflow.

---

## Example data and analysis

Every section below post-processes the same `PKNCAresults` object, built from
the Theoph dataset. The interval requests the headline parameters plus the
regression- and extrapolation-quality metrics that the exclusion demos rely on (`span.ratio`,
`adj.r.squared`, `aucpext.obs`):

```{r}
d_conc <- as.data.frame(Theoph) |> rename(time = Time, subject = Subject)
d_dose <- Theoph |> as.data.frame() |>
  group_by(Subject) |>
  summarise(dose = Dose[1] * Wt[1], weight = Wt[1], .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(subject = Subject) |>
  mutate(time = 0)

o_conc <- PKNCAconc(d_conc, conc ~ time | subject)
o_dose <- PKNCAdose(d_dose, dose ~ time | subject, route = "extravascular")
o_data <- PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose, intervals = data.frame(
  start = 0, end = Inf,
  auclast = TRUE, aucinf.obs = TRUE, cmax = TRUE,
  half.life = TRUE, span.ratio = TRUE, adj.r.squared = TRUE,
  aucpext.obs = TRUE
))
o_nca <- pk.nca(o_data)
```

---

## Extracting results

`as.data.frame()` returns the full tidy result including excluded rows:

```{r}
df <- as.data.frame(o_nca)

# Columns:
# subject    — group identifier
# start/end  — interval boundaries
# PPTESTCD   — parameter code
# PPORRES    — numeric result
# exclude    — NA if valid; character reason if excluded

df |>
  filter(PPTESTCD == "auclast") |>
  select(subject, PPORRES, exclude) |>
  arrange(subject)
```

---

## Excluding results

### Manual exclusion with `exclude()`

`exclude()` takes your results object plus a `reason` string and either a logical `mask` or a rule `FUN`. A manual `mask` excludes exactly the rows you flag — it does not propagate to other parameters. Rule-based exclusion (next section) does propagate: each rule excludes its affected parameters and the parameters that depend on them.

```{r}
# Exclude subject 3's half-life manually (e.g. failed QC review)
o_nca_excl <- exclude(
  o_nca,
  reason = "half-life failed manual QC",
  mask   = as.data.frame(o_nca)$subject == "3" &
           as.data.frame(o_nca)$PPTESTCD == "half.life"
)

# Only the masked half.life row is excluded
as.data.frame(o_nca_excl) |>
  filter(subject == "3", !is.na(exclude)) |>
  select(subject, PPTESTCD, PPORRES, exclude)
```

The function given as `FUN` (next section) is called once per group of results and must return either one value or one value per result row of the group; anything else is the `pknca_error_exclude_fun_length` error (≥ 0.13.0). A warning that the function signals reaches the caller with its class and fields intact (≥ 0.13.0), so it can be caught with `withCallingHandlers()`.

### Rule-based exclusion functions

PKNCA provides ready-made rule functions to pass to `exclude(FUN=...)`. Unlike a manual `mask`, rule-based exclusion propagates: each rule excludes the parameters it affects (for the half-life rules, the whole λz family) *and* the parameters that depend on them, such as `aucinf.obs` and `aucpext.obs`. The built-in rules also supply their own reason text, which overrides the `reason` argument in the `exclude` column.

| Function | Excludes when... |
|---|---|
| `exclude_nca_span.ratio(min.span.ratio)` | span.ratio < `min.span.ratio` (default from `PKNCA.options("min.span.ratio")`) |
| `exclude_nca_min.hl.r.squared(min.hl.r.squared)` | half-life unadjusted R² < `min.hl.r.squared` (default from `PKNCA.options("min.hl.r.squared")`) |
| `exclude_nca_min.hl.adj.r.squared(min.hl.adj.r.squared = 0.9)` | half-life adjusted R² < `min.hl.adj.r.squared` (stricter: adjusted for the number of points) |
| `exclude_nca_max.aucinf.pext(max.aucinf.pext)` | %AUCextrap > `max.aucinf.pext` (default from `PKNCA.options("max.aucinf.pext")`) |
| `exclude_nca_tmax_0()` | Tmax at or before 0 (shortcut for `exclude_nca_tmax_early(0)`) |
| `exclude_nca_tmax_early(tmax_early = 0)` | Tmax at or before a threshold time (`tmax_early`, default 0) |
| `exclude_nca_count_conc_measured(min_count, exclude_param_pattern = ...)` | fewer than `min_count` measured concentrations; excludes the AUC-family parameters matching `exclude_param_pattern` |
| `exclude_nca_by_param(parameter, min_thr = NULL, max_thr = NULL, affected_parameters = parameter)` (≥ 0.12.1) | the value of `parameter` falls outside `[min_thr, max_thr]`; excludes `affected_parameters` (default: `parameter` itself) |
| `exclude_nca_tmax_coverage(min_subjects = 4, k_warn = 1.5, k_exclude = 3)` (≥ 0.13.0) | the subject has no sample within Tukey's outer fences around its group's Tmax values; excludes every result of the interval (subjects outside only the inner fences get a warning) |

`pknca_exclude_rules()` (≥ 0.13.0) lists these rules with their arguments, defaults, the options they use, and the parameters each can exclude. The Tmax-coverage rule and the rule listing are demonstrated in the [Data Quality Checks chapter](data-quality.qmd).

```{r}
# Exclude half-lives where span ratio < 2
o_nca_span <- exclude(
  o_nca,
  reason = "span.ratio < 2",
  FUN    = exclude_nca_span.ratio(2)
)

as.data.frame(o_nca_span) |>
  filter(PPTESTCD == "half.life") |>
  select(subject, PPORRES, exclude) |>
  arrange(subject)
```

```{r}
# Propagation: subject 9 fails the span-ratio rule, so the entire lambda.z
# family and the parameters that depend on it are excluded together
as.data.frame(o_nca_span) |>
  filter(subject == "9", !is.na(exclude)) |>
  select(subject, PPTESTCD, exclude)
```

```{r}
# Chain multiple exclusion rules
o_nca_multi <- o_nca |>
  exclude(reason = "span.ratio < 2",    FUN = exclude_nca_span.ratio(2)) |>
  exclude(reason = "%AUCextrap > 20%",  FUN = exclude_nca_max.aucinf.pext(20))

as.data.frame(o_nca_multi) |>
  filter(!is.na(exclude)) |>
  select(subject, PPTESTCD, exclude) |>
  arrange(subject, PPTESTCD)
```

### Exclusions are respected in summary

Excluded values are dropped from the summary statistics: the parameters
affected by the span-ratio rule are summarized over fewer subjects, and the
caption defines the resulting `n=` annotation as the number of measurements
included in the summary.

```{r}
summary(o_nca_span)
```

---

## Dose-normalized parameters

PKNCA has built-in dose-normalized variants for several parameters. Request them in the interval — they are automatically computed as `parameter / dose`.

All available dose-normalized parameters, retrieved dynamically from the interval-column registry (`get.interval.cols()`):

```{r}
cols <- get.interval.cols()
dn_params <- names(cols)[endsWith(names(cols), ".dn")]
data.frame(
  parameter       = dn_params,
  description     = sapply(cols[dn_params], function(x) x$desc),
  normalized_from = sub("\\.dn$", "", dn_params)
) |> knitr::kable()
```

Each `.dn` parameter is computed as `parameter / dose` where `dose` is the dose from the `PKNCAdose` object for that interval. In PKNCA ≥ 0.13.0 this includes renal clearance variants (`clr.last.dn`, `clr.obs.dn`, `clr.pred.dn`).

Request the `.dn` variants in the interval like any other parameter:

```{r}
dn_interval <- data.frame(
  start           = 0,
  end             = Inf,
  auclast         = TRUE,
  auclast.dn      = TRUE,   # AUClast / dose
  aucinf.obs      = TRUE,
  aucinf.obs.dn   = TRUE,   # AUCinf.obs / dose
  aucinf.pred.dn  = TRUE,   # AUCinf.pred / dose
  cmax            = TRUE,
  cmax.dn         = TRUE,   # Cmax / dose
  cmin.dn         = TRUE,   # Cmin / dose
  aumclast.dn     = TRUE,   # AUMClast / dose
  clast.obs.dn    = TRUE,   # Clast.obs / dose
  cav.dn          = TRUE,   # Cav / dose
  half.life       = TRUE    # needed for aucinf.pred
)

o_nca_dn <- pk.nca(PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose, intervals = dn_interval))

as.data.frame(o_nca_dn) |>
  filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("auclast", "auclast.dn", "cmax", "cmax.dn",
                          "aucinf.obs", "aucinf.obs.dn")) |>
  select(subject, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = PPORRES) |>
  arrange(subject)
```

### Custom normalization with `normalize()` (≥ 0.13.0)

For normalization by columns other than dose (e.g. body weight, body surface area), PKNCA 0.13.0 adds `normalize()`. You supply a `norm_table` data frame containing the grouping columns, a `normalization` value, and a `unit` for each group. With grouped data, every group of the results must be in `norm_table`, so no result rows are dropped silently; with ungrouped data, `norm_table` must have exactly one row.

```{r}
# Normalize AUClast and Cmax by body weight
norm_tbl <- as.data.frame(Theoph) |>
  group_by(Subject) |>
  summarise(normalization = Wt[1], unit = "kg", .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(subject = Subject)

df_results <- as.data.frame(o_nca)
df_bw_norm <- normalize(
  df_results,
  norm_table  = norm_tbl,
  parameters  = c("auclast", "cmax"),
  suffix      = ".bw"
)

df_bw_norm |>
  select(subject, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  arrange(subject, PPTESTCD) |>
  head(8)
```

> `normalize()` returns **only** the normalized rows, under new parameter names — `auclast` becomes `auclast.bw`, `cmax` becomes `cmax.bw`. To keep both original and normalized values, bind the normalized rows onto the original results: `bind_rows(df_results, df_bw_norm)`.

`normalize()` also accepts the `PKNCAresults` object itself. It then adds the normalized rows to the results and returns a `PKNCAresults` object holding both the original and the normalized parameters (marked as modified; see the provenance note in the [Regulatory chapter](regulatory.qmd)).

### Normalizing by a column of the concentration data (≥ 0.13.0)

When the normalizing value is already a column of the concentration data, `normalize_by_col()` builds the normalization table from it. It takes a `PKNCAresults` object, the column name, and the unit (a fixed string or the name of a unit column), and returns a `PKNCAresults` object with the normalized parameters added. The Theoph concentration data carry body weight in `Wt`:

```{r}
o_nca_bw <- normalize_by_col(
  o_nca,
  col        = "Wt",
  unit       = "kg",
  parameters = c("auclast", "cmax"),
  suffix     = ".bw"
)

as.data.frame(o_nca_bw) |>
  filter(subject %in% c("1", "2"), PPTESTCD %in% c("auclast", "auclast.bw")) |>
  select(subject, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  arrange(subject, PPTESTCD)
```

Subject 1 weighs 79.6 kg, so its `auclast.bw` is its `auclast` divided by 79.6. The column must have one value per concentration group; a column whose value changes within a group (for example, a weight recorded at several visits within one profile) is the `pknca_error_norm_multiple_values` error.

---

## Filtering and grouping results

dplyr verbs work on `PKNCAresults` objects. `filter()` with expressions that use only group columns (the columns after the `|` in the `PKNCAconc()` formula) keeps the concentration data, dose data, and intervals in `$data` consistent with the remaining results (≥ 0.13.0); filters on other result columns (`PPTESTCD`, `PPORRES`, `exclude`) filter only the result table:

```{r}
o_nca_12 <- filter(o_nca, subject %in% c("1", "2"))
nrow(as.data.frame(o_nca_12))
unique(as.character(o_nca_12$data$conc$data$subject))
```

`group_vars()` on a `PKNCAresults` object includes the interval `start` and `end` with the group columns (≥ 0.13.0), so code that groups or joins results by `group_vars()` also matches on the interval:

```{r}
group_vars(o_nca)
```

A results object changed by `filter()`, `mutate()`, `exclude()`, or `normalize()` no longer passes `checkProvenance()`; see the [Regulatory chapter](regulatory.qmd#provenance-of-results).

---

## Controlling the summary table

`summary()` arguments control which groups and parameters appear and how gaps are shown:

| Argument | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `drop_group` | the subject column | Group columns summarized over (removed from the rows of the table) |
| `drop_param` | none | Parameters left out of the table |
| `summarize_n` | `NA` (add `N` when there is a subject column) | Add a column `N` with the number of subjects |
| `not_requested` | `"."` | Text for a parameter not requested in an interval |
| `not_calculated` | `"NC"` | Text for a requested parameter whose summary is `NA` |

```{r}
summary(o_nca, drop_param = c("adj.r.squared", "span.ratio"), summarize_n = FALSE)
```

When the summary shows the not-calculated text, the caption explains it (≥ 0.13.0). Here, a span-ratio threshold of 20 excludes every half-life, so the λz-dependent parameters are not calculated:

```{r}
summary(exclude(o_nca, FUN = exclude_nca_span.ratio(20)))
```

---

## Custom summary statistics

`PKNCA.set.summary()` controls how each parameter is presented in `summary()`.

```{r}
# Arithmetic mean ± SD for AUClast
PKNCA.set.summary(
  "auclast",
  description = "mean ± SD",
  point  = mean,
  spread = sd
)

# Median [min, max] for Tmax
# spread must return a 2-element numeric vector
PKNCA.set.summary(
  "tmax",
  description = "median [min, max]",
  point  = median,
  spread = function(x) c(min(x), max(x))
)

summary(o_nca)
```

`PKNCA.set.summary()` also has a `spread_for` argument (≥ 0.13.0) that summarizes one parameter with the spread taken from another parameter's results; PKNCA uses it to show a sparse AUClast as the estimate with its standard error (see the [Sparse NCA chapter](sparse.qmd)). `PKNCA.set.summary(reset = TRUE)` removes every summary instruction and, since that can break `summary()`, warns (≥ 0.13.0); restore individual parameters as below instead.

Restore the defaults — `business.geomean`/`business.geocv` for `auclast` and
`business.median`/`business.range` for `tmax` (the `business.*` helpers are
covered in the next section):

```{r}
PKNCA.set.summary(
  "auclast",
  description = "geometric mean and geometric coefficient of variation",
  point  = business.geomean,
  spread = business.geocv
)

PKNCA.set.summary(
  "tmax",
  description = "median and range",
  point  = business.median,
  spread = business.range
)
```

---

## Business summary helpers

PKNCA exports the full set of `business.*` summary functions. These are the defaults `summary()` uses for most parameters, and they are also available directly for custom reporting pipelines.

| Function | Returns | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `business.geomean(x)` | scalar | Geometric mean: exp(mean(log(x))) |
| `business.geocv(x)` | scalar | Geometric CV%: sqrt(exp(var(log(x)))−1) × 100 |
| `business.mean(x)` | scalar | Arithmetic mean |
| `business.sd(x)` | scalar | Standard deviation |
| `business.cv(x)` | scalar | Coefficient of variation %: sd/mean × 100 |
| `business.median(x)` | scalar | Median |
| `business.min(x)` | scalar | Minimum |
| `business.max(x)` | scalar | Maximum |
| `business.range(x)` | length-2 vector | c(min, max) |

```{r}
x <- c(10.2, 11.8, 9.6, 12.1, 10.5)
data.frame(
  statistic = c("geomean", "geocv", "mean", "sd", "cv%", "median", "min", "max"),
  value = c(
    business.geomean(x), business.geocv(x),
    business.mean(x),    business.sd(x),    business.cv(x),
    business.median(x),  business.min(x),   business.max(x)
  )
)
```

The `business.*` functions return `NA` for an empty input (≥ 0.13.0), rather than an error, so a summary group with no included values gives `NC` instead of stopping:

```{r}
business.geomean(numeric(0))
```

Use these as `point` and `spread` arguments to `PKNCA.set.summary()` — rerunning `summary()` shows the new `cmax` presentation:

```{r}
# Arithmetic mean ± CV% for Cmax
PKNCA.set.summary(
  "cmax",
  description = "mean [CV%]",
  point  = business.mean,
  spread = business.cv
)

summary(o_nca)
```

---

## Inspecting the terminal regression window

`get_halflife_points()` returns a logical vector aligned with the original concentration data — `TRUE` if that observation was used in the λz regression, `FALSE` if it was available but excluded, `NA` if half-life was not computed for that interval. In PKNCA ≥ 0.13.0 it also accepts a `PKNCAdata` object directly, handles `start ≠ 0` intervals correctly, and sets points outside any interval to `NA`. For how PKNCA selects the regression points, see the [Half-Life Calculation vignette](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v06-half-life-calculation.html).

Because the example analysis requested `half.life`, `o_nca` already carries the λz fits:

```{r}
# Logical vector (TRUE = used in lambda.z fit), aligned with the rows of d_conc
hl_used <- get_halflife_points(o_nca)
table(hl_used, useNA = "always")
```

```{r}
# >= 0.13.0: a PKNCAdata object is accepted directly (no need to run pk.nca first)
head(get_halflife_points(o_data))
```

`get_halflife_fit()` (≥ 0.13.0) returns the fitted terminal line of each interval (intercept and slope on the natural-log scale, and the first and last times used), and `get_halflife_curve()` (≥ 0.13.0) returns predicted concentrations along it, by default `n = 50` points from the first time used, extrapolated to the end of the interval's data (`extrapolate_later = TRUE`):

```{r}
get_halflife_fit(o_nca) |> filter(subject == "1")
d_hl_curve <- get_halflife_curve(o_nca)
head(d_hl_curve |> filter(subject == "1"), 3)
```

```{r}
# Attach to concentration data for plotting
d_conc_annotated <- d_conc |> mutate(in_lambda_z = hl_used)
subj1_conc <- d_conc_annotated |> filter(subject == "1")

ggplot(subj1_conc, aes(x = time, y = conc, colour = in_lambda_z)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(data = d_hl_curve |> filter(subject == "1"), colour = "firebrick",
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "grey50", "TRUE" = "firebrick"),
                      labels = c("not used", "used in lambda.z"), name = NULL,
                      na.value = "grey80") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Subject 1 - points used in lambda.z regression (red) and fitted line",
       x = "Time (h)", y = "Concentration (mg/L) [log scale]") +
  theme_minimal()
```

---

## Imputation methods

Imputation is a pre-calculation step, not a post-processing step. It is specified before `pk.nca()` runs via the `impute` argument to `PKNCAdata()` — either a method name applied to every interval, or the name of a column in the intervals data frame holding per-interval methods. See the [Concentration Imputation chapter](imputation.qmd) for the built-in strategies, chaining, custom methods, and a side-by-side comparison.
